title: Ace Hunting: Probabilities in a Deck of Cards

body.heading: Four aces in fifty-two
paragraphs: A standard deck holds 52 cards and 4 aces, so the chance that a single drawn card is an ace is 4 out of 52, which simplifies to 1 in 13 - about 7.7 percent. Clean, simple, and true only while the deck is complete.

The moment a card leaves the deck, the odds move. Draw a card that is not an ace and the chance the next card is an ace rises slightly, to 4 in 51. Draw an ace first and the chance falls to 3 in 51. Drawing without replacement means every card you have seen is information, and the probabilities update to match.

body.heading: Two aces in a row
paragraphs: What about drawing two aces back to back? Multiply the changing odds: 4/52 for the first, then 3/51 for the second. The result is 12 out of 2,652, which simplifies to 1 in 221 - under half of one percent. Rare, but not miraculous: deal two cards to enough pairs of players and it will happen regularly.

Compare that with putting the first card back and shuffling, where the second draw stays 4/52 and the pair comes out at 1 in 169. Replacement keeps the world unchanged; without replacement, the deck remembers - and skilled card players are, at heart, people who track what the deck remembers.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Shuffle a deck, predict 'ace or not' before each draw, and draw ten cards without replacing them, keeping a tally. Then work out what the ace probability was before each draw, given the cards already out. Notice how your predictions could have improved by simply counting.
Try the same tally for hearts, where you start with 13 chances in 52. The bigger target makes the updating effect easier to see in a short experiment.

takeaway: Cards that have left the deck change the odds for the next draw - counting what has gone is the first skill of card probability.
